transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I’m here because things at work have gotten to a point where I just can't ignore what's happening anymore. I'm a mathematician, you see, and I’ve been leading this major environmental modeling contract. It's incredibly complex work, predictive algorithms, massive datasets, the kind of thing where precision is everything. But lately, well, for a while now, actually, I’m pretty sure—no, I know—that the people on that contract, the other stakeholders, they’ve been tracking my revisions. And not just tracking them, they are actively planting errors in the datasets. 

I’ll run a model, perfectly calibrated, and the next day, the variables are skewed. The code is altered. They’re doing it deliberately to make it look like I’m losing my edge, like I can’t lead the work anymore. I’ve tried explaining this, I really have. I’ve showed the logs to the junior analysts, and I’ve even tried to explain it to my wife, but they just... they don't see it. Or they refuse to see it. They keep telling me, "Oh, it’s just version-control mistakes," or "Someone just overwrote the file by accident." But you don't just 'accidentally' introduce a systematic bias into a stochastic model, doctor. It takes intent. It takes planning. And they're doing it to push me out, I just know it. It's exhausting, having to constantly double-check every single line of data just to prove I'm not the one making these so-called mistakes.
Have you been feeling unusually high or euphoric lately?

Euphoric? High? No, doctor, no, not at all. I mean, how could I possibly feel euphoric? If anything, it's the exact opposite, though I wouldn't say I'm depressed either, just... constantly vigilant. You have to understand the sheer mental toll it takes to be on guard like this. When you're dealing with predictive algorithms, you have to hold so many variables in your head at once, and when you add the layer of knowing that someone—multiple someones, really—are actively working to undermine that... well, there's no room for euphoria. 

There's no time to feel high or elated when you're spending your evenings, your weekends, the hours when you're supposed to be sleeping, just pouring over lines of code, looking for the traps they've set. I remember just last Tuesday, I was looking at this one specific subroutine, and I thought, for just a fraction of a second, I thought I'd finally caught them out, found the exact IP address of the person making the changes, and I suppose you could say I felt a brief flash of satisfaction, maybe a bit of relief, but it certainly wasn't euphoria. It was just the grim satisfaction of knowing I wasn't crazy, before the reality set back in that I still had to prove it to people who refuse to look at the evidence. So, no, no highs. Just a very steady, very exhausting baseline of having to protect my work and my reputation from these relentless attacks.
Have you had any recent neurological illness or head injury?

A head injury? Neurological illness? No, no, certainly not. I mean, my brain is my livelihood, doctor. If there were something physically wrong with my head, some sort of... neurological deficit, I would be the very first to know. You can’t run complex predictive modeling if your synapses aren't firing exactly as they should. I haven't hit my head, I haven't been in any accidents, no strokes or... or anything like that. In fact, I just saw my general practitioner a few months ago for my annual physical, and everything was completely normal. Blood pressure, reflexes, all of it perfectly fine. 

If I were neurologically compromised, do you really think I’d be able to spot a fraction of a percent deviation in a stochastic matrix? Of course not. I'd be making the mistakes myself. And frankly, I think that's exactly what those people on the contract are hoping everyone will think. If they can just introduce enough errors into my code, maybe management will start asking if I'm getting too old, if my mind is slipping at sixty, if I've had some sort of... of cognitive decline or silent illness. But my mind is incredibly sharp. It has to be, just to catch what they're doing behind my back. I spend hours tracing the logic pathways, and my math is flawless every single time. It's the external inputs that are tainted, not my head. So, no, absolutely no head injuries or illnesses. Just a perfectly healthy brain that is being forced to work overtime to defend its own work.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Voices? Like... hallucinating voices? No, doctor, no. I'm not hearing things. I know it might sound like I'm under a lot of stress, and I am, but I'm not losing my grip on reality like that. I don't hear people whispering in my ear when the room is empty, or... or disembodied voices telling me what to do. 

The only voices I hear are the very real ones of my colleagues during our weekly status meetings, and even then, it's what they aren't saying that's the problem. They sit there, nodding, agreeing with my projections, and then the minute the call ends, they're back in the system, altering the parameters. But as for actual, auditory hallucinations? No, absolutely not. My office is perfectly quiet when I'm working alone. In fact, the silence is almost deafening sometimes, especially late at night when I'm staring at the screen, just waiting to see if the file size changes, indicating someone has accessed the server. But no voices. Just the hum of my computer tower and the occasional car driving by outside. I'm completely grounded in reality, doctor. It's the reality of my situation that's the problem, not my perception of it.
How long have you been convinced that people at work are deliberately sabotaging your data?

Well, it hasn't been forever, if that's what you're asking. It's not like I've spent my entire career looking over my shoulder. I've been doing this kind of modeling for decades, and for the most part, people respect the math. But this specific situation... this absolute certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions, that they are actively, deliberately planting errors in the code to make me look incompetent... that really crystallized about two months ago. 

I mean, I can trace it back to the exact week. It was right around the end of the first quarter, when we were supposed to be finalizing the predictive models for the new rollout. I had submitted my data—clean, verified, mathematically sound data—on a Thursday afternoon. And by Monday morning, when we had the review, the entire matrix was skewed. At first, I thought it was a system glitch, you know? A server error, a corrupted file during the upload process. You always want to assume the best, or at least the most logical, non-malicious explanation. So I spent that entire Monday, probably fourteen hours straight, just combing through the logs, trying to find the point of failure. 

And that's when I saw it. The timestamps. Someone had been in there on Sunday night, around 11:30 PM, making microscopic adjustments to the weighting algorithms. Just enough to throw the final projections off by a few percentage points, but not enough to trigger the automated error flags. It was surgical, doctor. Absolutely surgical. And ever since that moment, for the last two months, it's been a constant battle. I fix it, they break it. I lock the file, they find a backdoor. It's been eight weeks of this relentless, exhausting back-and-forth, and management just turns a blind eye to it all. So, yes, two months of knowing exactly what they're doing.
Have you had the feeling that an outside force is controlling your thoughts or actions?

Controlling my thoughts? Or my actions? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, that sounds like something out of a science fiction movie, doctor, someone having their mind controlled by some invisible force or a microchip or whatever it is people come up with. No, my thoughts are entirely my own. In fact, they have to be. If I weren't in complete control of my own cognitive processes, I wouldn't be able to stay ahead of what's happening at work. 

Every action I take, every line of code I write, every security protocol I implement—it's all me. It's my logic, my reasoning, my mathematical background driving those decisions. If someone else were controlling me, they wouldn't be doing it to protect the data, would they? They'd be making me sabotage my own work, which is exactly what I'm fighting against. I am fully autonomous. I decide when I log in, I decide when I run the diagnostics, I decide when to re-verify the stochastic variables. Sometimes I decide to stay up until three in the morning because I know that's when they like to try and slip past the firewall, but that's my choice. It's a choice born of necessity, of course, because if I don't do it, no one will, but it is my choice nonetheless. 

So, no, there's no outside force pulling my strings or putting thoughts in my head. My thoughts are perfectly clear, perfectly rational, and entirely generated by my own brain. The only outside force I'm dealing with is the very real, very tangible interference from my colleagues trying to ruin my models. But my mind? My actions? Those are completely under my control. I wouldn't have survived this long in my field if they weren't.
Has anyone told you recently that your speech or thoughts seem confused or hard to follow?

Confused? Hard to follow? No. No, not at all. I mean, certainly not in the way you're implying. Look, doctor, I work in mathematical sciences. I've spent my entire adult life—well, ever since I took those advanced calculus and statistical modeling courses back when I was at the university—I've spent decades communicating in a language of precision. Variables, parameters, standard deviations... these aren't things you can just be "confused" about. You're either right or you're wrong. The math is either sound or it's flawed.

So when I explain things, when I lay out the timeline of how they are manipulating the server logs, I am being as precise as a metronome. I give them the exact timestamps, the specific algorithmic shifts, the exact percentage point deviations. If anything, I'm too detailed for them. Management doesn't want to hear about stochastic weighting, they just want a green light on a spreadsheet. So if they say I'm "hard to follow," it's simply because they don't have the technical vocabulary to keep up with the data I'm presenting. It's a deficit on their end, not mine. 

I mean, just last week, I sat down with the project lead—well, virtually sat down, on a video call—and I walked him through the entire sequence of unauthorized edits from the previous Sunday. I had it all mapped out. I showed him how the backdoor was accessed, how the variables were inverted, the whole chain of events. And he just stared at me, blinking, and said, "I think you're overcomplicating things." Overcomplicating! I was giving him the exact mechanism of the sabotage! It's not my fault if the reality of what's happening is complex. The truth is often complex. But my explanation of it? Perfectly logical. Perfectly linear. I haven't had a single person tell me my thoughts are confused, because they aren't. They're just... they're just willfully ignoring the facts I'm laying out right in front of them.
Before these last two months, had you had any similar beliefs that other people were deliberately plotting against you?

Well, not exactly like this, no. Not this... this surgical level of interference. But if you're asking if I've noticed a pattern, a shift in how people operate around me... yes. Yes, I suppose you could say there's a broader timeline here. It wasn't just a sudden switch that flipped two months ago, even though that's when the undeniable proof in the server logs appeared. The foundation for all of this, the... the groundwork, if you will, that started much earlier. 

If I really think about it, and I have—I've spent hours analyzing the sequence of events, mapping the trajectory of how the workplace dynamics deteriorated—this whole decline started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract. That was about two years and two months ago. Exactly twenty-six months, give or take a few days depending on when the paperwork officially cleared HR. 

Before that contract, I was mostly handling localized data sets. Smaller teams, less visibility, less... less threat to the established hierarchy, I suppose. But when they handed me the environmental modeling project, it was a massive upgrade in responsibility. The data sets were enormous, spanning decades of climate variables, soil erosion metrics, atmospheric pressure shifts... it required a level of precision that frankly, most people in that office just aren't capable of maintaining. I had to restructure the entire analytical framework from the ground up just to ensure the integrity of the predictive algorithms. 

And almost immediately—within weeks of me taking the helm—I noticed the shift. It wasn't outright sabotage then, not like the algorithmic tampering I'm dealing with now. It was more insidious. Passive-aggressive resistance. People "forgetting" to cc me on crucial correspondence regarding data collection methodologies. Subordinates submitting raw data that was formatted in ways they knew would crash my initial sorting scripts, forcing me to spend hours reformatting everything manually. I remember one specific instance, maybe a year and a half ago, where a junior analyst—who had a master's degree, mind you, so he wasn't incompetent—submitted a batch of oceanic temperature readings where the decimal points were shifted exactly one place to the left. Just enough to look like a clerical error, but if I hadn't caught it, it would have invalidated six months of projections. 

So, was it a deliberate plot back then? They'd call it incompetence if you pressed them. They'd say they were overworked or misunderstood the parameters. But I know math, doctor. I know probability. And the probability of that many "mistakes" happening consistently, always in a way that specifically hindered my progress on the environmental contract... it's statistically improbable. It was a concerted effort to undermine my authority and slow down the project. They didn't have the technical skills to break my models back then, so they tried to drown me in administrative and clerical sabotage. The outright tampering I've seen over the last two months? That's just the evolution of what started two years and two months ago. It's the same agenda, just a different, more aggressive tactic.
Aside from this problem at work, have you become less able to manage your usual daily life than before?

Well, you say aside from work, but frankly, doctor, the two are inextricably linked. The fallout from what's happening at the office bleeds into everything else. But... yes. Yes, I suppose if we are looking at the overall metrics of my day-to-day functioning, there has been a... a degradation. 

Even just looking at the practical output at work, because of all the time I have to spend verifying and re-verifying the data to counter their interference, I’ve actually fallen quite far behind on the primary modeling deliverables. It's a simple issue of bandwidth. If I'm spending eighty percent of my time playing defense against unauthorized edits, the actual production suffers. It got to the point recently where the firm actually stepped in and reassigned pieces of my contract to other teams. Just carved it up and handed it off, which is incredibly frustrating. And the junior analysts I’m supposed to be supervising... I’ve essentially stopped being useful to them. I just don't have the time to review their preliminary scripts or hold their hands through basic statistical regressions anymore because I'm too busy trying to keep the core architecture from collapsing. 

And that level of constant, high-alert cognitive load... it doesn't just vanish when I shut my laptop. When I'm at home, I find I just... I mostly keep to myself. I retreat to the study. The baseline variables of daily life, the routine maintenance, it just falls by the wayside. My wife, bless her, she's had to really push me lately just to keep basic routines going. I mean things like remembering to come down and sit at the table for dinner, or taking the recycling out, or even just keeping up with getting dressed properly on a Sunday morning. She has to remind me, sometimes multiple times, because my mind is entirely occupied. I'm running mental simulations on how to secure the server, so I just can't be bothered with mundane domestic tasks. So, yes, my ability to manage the usual daily schedule has slipped. It's collateral damage, really.
Has anyone close to you noticed that you’ve become more emotionally flat or less expressive than you used to be?

My wife, yes, she has said things to that effect. She tells me I seem flat, or that I am a million miles away, that I don't react to things or show enthusiasm the way I used to. And I suppose, if we are looking at it purely from an observational standpoint, her assessment of my external behavior is accurate. 

I can tell you what she is seeing. These days, I can just sit. Literally just sit in one place, for hours on end. Sometimes I am at my desk, but often I will just go out to the garage. I have a rather sophisticated telescope out there—a beautiful piece of equipment, excellent optics for deep-sky observation—and I will just sit in a folding chair right next to it, with the canvas dust cover still on. I don't even bother to unbuckle the cover. I just sit there in the dim light.

It is a stark contrast to my previous baseline, I will readily admit that. If you looked at my schedule even a few years ago, I was highly engaged. I used to really enjoy hiking, taking the trails up the northern ridge where the elevation gain requires a very calculated, steady pace. And as I mentioned before, I used to take real pride in mentoring the younger analysts at the firm, guiding them through complex data structures and predictive modeling. I even used to go to these community astronomy nights, set up my equipment in the park, and talk to complete strangers for hours about celestial mechanics and orbital trajectories. 

But now... I know I used to enjoy those things. I retain the factual memory of enjoying them. But the... the activation energy just isn't there anymore. I just don't feel much pull to start anything, or even to talk to anyone. The desire to explain things, to engage, to participate in the world outside of the immediate data I am processing... it has just evaporated. So I sit in the garage, looking at a covered telescope, and my wife sees a man who has lost his expressiveness. But really, I just don't feel the necessary internal momentum to participate in any of it anymore.
For at least one full month, have you been convinced that your coworkers are deliberately sabotaging your work?

Well, yes. More than a month, certainly. If we are establishing a precise timeline here—the exact point where my working hypothesis transitioned into an undeniable, empirical fact—that certainty has been there for about the last two months. 

As I was explaining earlier, the groundwork, the passive resistance, that was laid much earlier. But the absolute certainty... the irrefutable proof that people on the project are actively, deliberately tracking my specific revisions in the system and intentionally planting errors into the data sets? That crystallized about two months ago. 

You see, when you really sit down and monitor the version control history, you start to notice the timestamps. It's quite revealing. They wait for me to commit a revision to the environmental model, and then, almost like clockwork, they go into the architecture and introduce these microscopic flaws. A transposed variable here, a corrupted syntax line there. It's not random system degradation. It takes a highly dedicated, coordinated effort to track someone's revisions that closely just to plant errors that are designed to look like my own mathematical oversights. 

It is incredibly tedious for me to have to go back and scrub the server logs line by line to find where they’ve been, which is why I'm so behind on the deliverables. But I have to do it, because if I don't catch the errors they plant, the entire predictive algorithm collapses. So, yes, to answer your question regarding the one-month threshold, it has been a solid two months of absolute certainty regarding this specific, targeted interference. I just can't fathom how they think I wouldn't notice the statistical impossibility of these errors generating themselves.
Do you ever feel that other people can hear or know your thoughts, even when you haven’t said them out loud?

Hear my thoughts? No, no, let's remain grounded in the physical parameters of reality here, doctor. I am a man of mathematics, of empirical data and structural realities. The human brain is a biological engine, a closed neural network, not some sort of unencrypted radio transmitter broadcasting on an open frequency. 

If my coworkers—or anyone else, for that matter—had the capacity to intercept my internal cognitive processes, well, the entire dynamic of their interference would be completely different, wouldn't it? Just think about the logistics of it. They wouldn't have to wait for me to commit a revision to the server to plant their errors. They would just anticipate my modeling strategies before I even touched the keyboard. They would preempt my equations entirely. But they don't do that. They are completely reliant on observing my external outputs, my keystrokes, my logged data. 

My mind is a secure, closed system. In fact, it is perhaps the only environment I have left that hasn't been compromised by unauthorized access. I mean, consider the physics of what you're asking. Telepathy is a science fiction construct, a complete statistical impossibility without some sort of invasive neuro-technological interface, which I obviously do not possess. Now, could they be attempting behavioral prediction based on a statistical analysis of my past actions? Certainly. That's just basic predictive modeling, anyone with a decent background in algorithmic forecasting could attempt that. But literally hearing my thoughts as they form in my cerebral cortex? No, absolutely not. 

I keep my internal variables strictly compartmentalized. They only know what I execute, not what I am contemplating. If they could hear my thoughts, I wouldn't be able to sit out in the garage and run my mental simulations in peace, because they'd already be formulating their counter-measures to my security protocols before I even implemented them. So, no, I can say with absolute empirical certainty that my thoughts remain entirely my own. That is one boundary they cannot cross.
At any point, have these problems been at their worst continuously for a full month or more?

Well, yes, if we are looking at the continuous nature of the situation, the timeline is quite clear. I believe I touched on this a moment ago, but to be absolutely precise regarding your parameters of a "full month or more," the answer is unequivocally affirmative. 

The certainty—the absolute, empirical certainty that these individuals on the project are actively tracking my specific revisions in the system and intentionally planting these microscopic errors into the data sets—that has been a constant, unyielding reality for about the last two months. And I don't use the word "constant" lightly, doctor. I am talking about a continuous, day-in, day-out barrage of interference. There hasn't been a single day in the past sixty days where I could log into the server and not find evidence of their tampering. 

It is a relentless cycle. I wake up, I go to my desk, I open the version control history, and there it is. The corrupted syntax, the transposed variables, always timed perfectly after my commits. And because it is so continuous, my response to it has to be equally continuous. I am constantly in a state of having to scrub the server logs, line by tedious line, just to keep the predictive algorithm from collapsing entirely. So, to address your question of whether it has been at its worst continuously for a month or more... yes. The last two months have been an unbroken continuum of this targeted sabotage. There has been no reprieve, no pause in their efforts, and consequently, no pause in my need to counteract them. It is a highly demanding, ongoing variable in my daily calculations.
For at least six months, have you had ongoing problems like this—feeling people are plotting against you or that your work is being sabotaged?

Well, six months... six months is a gross underestimation of the timeline we're dealing with here, doctor. If we are tracking the actual trajectory of this... this organized resistance, we have to look much further back. The two months of absolute, undeniable sabotage I just described? That's merely the apex of the curve. The current, most aggressive manifestation of a systemic issue that has been compounding for quite some time.

If you want the true origin point, the moment the variables shifted and the environment became hostile... well, you have to look at the project timeline. This whole decline, this orchestrated effort to undermine my methodologies, it started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract. That was, let me think... yes, about two years and two months ago. 

I remember it quite distinctly, because the parameters of my responsibilities expanded exponentially, and almost immediately, I noticed a shift in the workplace dynamics. It started with subtle things, you know? Passive-aggressive delays in data handoffs, "misplaced" reference files, emails that supposedly went to my spam folder but were clearly never sent. At the time, I tried to model it as standard workplace friction, perhaps professional jealousy over the contract assignment. It's a massive project, highly visible, with significant funding attached. It would be statistically probable to encounter some level of resentment. 

But as the months progressed, the friction evolved into friction by design. It wasn't just inefficiency; it was targeted inefficiency. They were testing the boundaries of my oversight, seeing how much they could disrupt the workflow without leaving a definitive digital footprint. For over a year and a half, it was this low-grade, simmering campaign to isolate me and compromise the integrity of the preliminary models. I spent countless hours recalibrating my expectations of their output, trying to factor their "incompetence" into my equations. 

So, yes, to answer your question about the six-month threshold... we crossed that line a long, long time ago. It has been over two years of escalating interference, culminating in this current, highly aggressive phase of direct code manipulation that I've been battling for the last two months. It's a long-term, sustained operation, doctor, not some recent development.
Have you been neglecting basic personal hygiene, like bathing or changing clothes, more than you used to?

Neglecting my hygiene? No. No, I find that line of inquiry a bit perplexing, to be perfectly frank, doctor. Why would I alter my baseline physical maintenance protocols? I am a man of structure. My morning routine is a highly calibrated sequence of events, and it has not deviated in the slightest. 

I wake up at precisely 5:30 AM every single day. I proceed immediately to the washroom for a fifteen-minute shower—water temperature regulated, of course. I utilize the same unscented soap, the same standard shaving cream, because introducing new, unpredictable chemical variables into my morning routine is entirely unnecessary. I launder my garments every Sunday afternoon, separating them by fabric weight and color saturation to ensure maximum longevity of the materials. So, my clothes are clean, my person is clean. The structural integrity of my personal upkeep remains at exactly one hundred percent.

If anything, maintaining a strict adherence to these physical parameters is more important now than ever before. Just think about the optics of the situation. If I were to let my personal upkeep degrade—if I started showing up to the project meetings looking disheveled, or wearing the same shirt three days in a row—what do you think the immediate calculation on their end would be? They would log that data. They would see it as a quantifiable metric that their campaign of sabotage is successfully breaking down my operational capacity. They would interpret a wrinkled collar or an unshaven jaw as a definitive sign of systemic collapse. 

I absolutely refuse to provide them with that kind of empirical satisfaction. I will not hand them the data points they so desperately want. My cognitive faculties are functioning at an optimal level, and my external presentation must reflect that internal order. I am not some chaotic, unspooled variable in this equation, doctor. I am the control. So, no, bathing, changing clothes... all of that is executed with the exact same precision it always has been. There has been zero degradation in my personal hygiene.

At any time during this, have you had a period of at least a month when, in addition to believing your coworkers were sabotaging you, you also had another symptom like hearing voices, disorganized speech, or feeling emotionally flat?

Well... it's interesting you bring up the concept of emotional flatness, or a lack of drive, because... well, yes. Yes, I suppose that is a variable that has entered the equation over the last several months. It's not the voices or the disorganized speech you mentioned—my cognitive processes, as I've demonstrated, are entirely intact and structured. But the... the motivation, the internal catalyst for action, that has certainly degraded.

It’s a very specific phenomenon. I find myself, quite frequently these days, just sitting. I can sit for hours at my desk, looking at the monitor without actually initiating a task, or I’ll go out to the garage where I keep my equipment. I have a very fine telescope out there, a Schmidt-Cassegrain model, precisely calibrated. I used to be quite involved in the local astronomy nights, setting it up, explaining the orbital mechanics to the laypeople... I enjoyed that. I used to enjoy a lot of things. Hiking the trails up by the ridge, calculating the elevation gains and pacing myself... I used to mentor the younger analysts at the firm, too, before they all turned on me, of course. I took pride in showing them how to construct a truly elegant predictive model.

But now? Now I can sit in that garage for three, four hours at a time, and the telescope stays covered the entire duration. I just sit there. I know, logically, that these are activities I previously derived satisfaction from. The data supports that conclusion. But the actual... the pull to do them? The desire to initiate the sequence of events required to go on a hike or attend a social function? It’s just... absent. It’s like a null value in the system. I don't feel the urge to start anything, and I certainly don't feel the urge to talk to anyone, given the current hostile parameters of my environment. It’s not sadness, exactly, doctor. It’s just a profound, pervasive emptiness where my drive used to be. A complete flattening of the emotional curve, if you will. And yes, that has been a consistent state of affairs for well over a month now, running concurrently with the... the other issues we've discussed.
For at least one full month, have you had this loss of motivation and emotional flatness?

Well, yes, doctor, as I... as I believe I just articulated a moment ago, we are well past the thirty-day mark on this particular data point. It has been a full month, absolutely. Probably closer to six weeks, if we were to graph it out accurately. 

As I was saying, I find myself in this state where I can just sit there. For hours at a time. I'll sit at my desk, or I'll go out to the garage, and the telescope—the Schmidt-Cassegrain I mentioned—it just sits there with the dust cover still on it. I can stare at it, and I know, intellectually, that I used to derive a significant amount of satisfaction from it. Going to the local astronomy nights, calibrating the lenses, explaining the orbital mechanics to the public... I know the data says I enjoyed that. Just like I know I used to enjoy hiking up the ridge and mapping out the elevation gains, or... or mentoring the younger analysts at the firm, back before the workplace dynamics shifted so drastically against me. 

But these days? I just don’t feel much pull to start anything. It's like a complete failure in the initiation sequence of my brain. There's no internal spark to begin an activity, and frankly, I don't feel any pull to talk to anyone either. The desire to engage, to initiate a project, to converse... it has just flatlined. It's a persistent, daily reality. So, yes, to confirm your specific timeline, it has absolutely been at least one full month of this... this null state.

So, no, I can say with absolute empirical certainty that my thoughts remain entirely my own. That is one boundary they cannot cross.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a continuous period of prominent psychotic symptoms lasting at least one month, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from acute psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: At any point, have these problems been at their worst continuously for a full month or more?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The certainty that people on the project are tracking my revisions and planting errors has been there for about the last two months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the severe symptoms (active phase) have lasted for a full month or more, which corresponds to the duration of my psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, if we are looking at the continuous nature of the situation, the timeline is quite clear. I believe I touched on this a moment ago, but to be absolutely precise regarding your parameters of a "full month or more," the answer is unequivocally affirmative. 

The certainty—the absolute, empirical certainty that these individuals on the project are actively tracking my specific revisions in the system and intentionally planting these microscopic errors into the data sets—that has been a constant, unyielding reality for about the last two months. And I don't use the word "constant" lightly, doctor. I am talking about a continuous, day-in, day-out barrage of interference. There hasn't been a single day in the past sixty days where I could log into the server and not find evidence of their tampering. 

It is a relentless cycle. I wake up, I go to my desk, I open the version control history, and there it is. The corrupted syntax, the transposed variables, always timed perfectly after my commits. And because it is so continuous, my response to it has to be equally continuous. I am constantly in a state of having to scrub the server logs, line by tedious line, just to keep the predictive algorithm from collapsing entirely. So, to address your question of whether it has been at its worst continuously for a month or more... yes. The last two months have been an unbroken continuum of this targeted sabotage. There has been no reprieve, no pause in their efforts, and consequently, no pause in my need to counteract them. It is a highly demanding, ongoing variable in my daily calculations.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least six months, which best distinguishes schizophrenia from delusional disorder or acute polymorphic psychotic disorder with schizophrenic symptoms.
doctor.question: For at least six months, have you had ongoing problems like this—feeling people are plotting against you or that your work is being sabotaged?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This whole decline started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract about two years and two months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if the problems (like feeling people are plotting against him or work being sabotaged) have been ongoing for at least six months. This directly relates to the 'Duration' of the overall decline/illness, which the patient profile lists as '2 years and 2 months'.

patient.answer:
Well, six months... six months is a gross underestimation of the timeline we're dealing with here, doctor. If we are tracking the actual trajectory of this... this organized resistance, we have to look much further back. The two months of absolute, undeniable sabotage I just described? That's merely the apex of the curve. The current, most aggressive manifestation of a systemic issue that has been compounding for quite some time.

If you want the true origin point, the moment the variables shifted and the environment became hostile... well, you have to look at the project timeline. This whole decline, this orchestrated effort to undermine my methodologies, it started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract. That was, let me think... yes, about two years and two months ago. 

I remember it quite distinctly, because the parameters of my responsibilities expanded exponentially, and almost immediately, I noticed a shift in the workplace dynamics. It started with subtle things, you know? Passive-aggressive delays in data handoffs, "misplaced" reference files, emails that supposedly went to my spam folder but were clearly never sent. At the time, I tried to model it as standard workplace friction, perhaps professional jealousy over the contract assignment. It's a massive project, highly visible, with significant funding attached. It would be statistically probable to encounter some level of resentment. 

But as the months progressed, the friction evolved into friction by design. It wasn't just inefficiency; it was targeted inefficiency. They were testing the boundaries of my oversight, seeing how much they could disrupt the workflow without leaving a definitive digital footprint. For over a year and a half, it was this low-grade, simmering campaign to isolate me and compromise the integrity of the preliminary models. I spent countless hours recalibrating my expectations of their output, trying to factor their "incompetence" into my equations. 

So, yes, to answer your question about the six-month threshold... we crossed that line a long, long time ago. It has been over two years of escalating interference, culminating in this current, highly aggressive phase of direct code manipulation that I've been battling for the last two months. It's a long-term, sustained operation, doctor, not some recent development.

inference.note: Duration of persecutory beliefs is now >2 years, which rules out acute/transient psychotic disorder (F23.3). Marked negative symptoms/functional decline keep schizophrenia (F20.0) in consideration, while persistent persecutory delusions without hallucinations remain consistent with delusional disorder (F22).

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a marked decline in self-care or hygiene, which would favor schizophrenia over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Have you been neglecting basic personal hygiene, like bathing or changing clothes, more than you used to?

patient.answer:
Neglecting my hygiene? No. No, I find that line of inquiry a bit perplexing, to be perfectly frank, doctor. Why would I alter my baseline physical maintenance protocols? I am a man of structure. My morning routine is a highly calibrated sequence of events, and it has not deviated in the slightest. 

I wake up at precisely 5:30 AM every single day. I proceed immediately to the washroom for a fifteen-minute shower—water temperature regulated, of course. I utilize the same unscented soap, the same standard shaving cream, because introducing new, unpredictable chemical variables into my morning routine is entirely unnecessary. I launder my garments every Sunday afternoon, separating them by fabric weight and color saturation to ensure maximum longevity of the materials. So, my clothes are clean, my person is clean. The structural integrity of my personal upkeep remains at exactly one hundred percent.

If anything, maintaining a strict adherence to these physical parameters is more important now than ever before. Just think about the optics of the situation. If I were to let my personal upkeep degrade—if I started showing up to the project meetings looking disheveled, or wearing the same shirt three days in a row—what do you think the immediate calculation on their end would be? They would log that data. They would see it as a quantifiable metric that their campaign of sabotage is successfully breaking down my operational capacity. They would interpret a wrinkled collar or an unshaven jaw as a definitive sign of systemic collapse. 

I absolutely refuse to provide them with that kind of empirical satisfaction. I will not hand them the data points they so desperately want. My cognitive faculties are functioning at an optimal level, and my external presentation must reflect that internal order. I am not some chaotic, unspooled variable in this equation, doctor. I am the control. So, no, bathing, changing clothes... all of that is executed with the exact same precision it always has been. There has been zero degradation in my personal hygiene.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has ever been a period of at least one month with psychotic symptoms outside the persecutory delusion, which would support schizophrenia over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: At any time during this, have you had a period of at least a month when, in addition to believing your coworkers were sabotaging you, you also had another symptom like hearing voices, disorganized speech, or feeling emotionally flat?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: These days I can sit for hours at my desk or in the garage with the telescope still covered, knowing I used to enjoy hiking, mentoring the younger analysts, and going to astronomy nights, but I just don’t feel much pull to start anything or talk to anyone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the presence of other symptoms such as feeling emotionally flat or lacking motivation, which corresponds directly to my negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well... it's interesting you bring up the concept of emotional flatness, or a lack of drive, because... well, yes. Yes, I suppose that is a variable that has entered the equation over the last several months. It's not the voices or the disorganized speech you mentioned—my cognitive processes, as I've demonstrated, are entirely intact and structured. But the... the motivation, the internal catalyst for action, that has certainly degraded.

It’s a very specific phenomenon. I find myself, quite frequently these days, just sitting. I can sit for hours at my desk, looking at the monitor without actually initiating a task, or I’ll go out to the garage where I keep my equipment. I have a very fine telescope out there, a Schmidt-Cassegrain model, precisely calibrated. I used to be quite involved in the local astronomy nights, setting it up, explaining the orbital mechanics to the laypeople... I enjoyed that. I used to enjoy a lot of things. Hiking the trails up by the ridge, calculating the elevation gains and pacing myself... I used to mentor the younger analysts at the firm, too, before they all turned on me, of course. I took pride in showing them how to construct a truly elegant predictive model.

But now? Now I can sit in that garage for three, four hours at a time, and the telescope stays covered the entire duration. I just sit there. I know, logically, that these are activities I previously derived satisfaction from. The data supports that conclusion. But the actual... the pull to do them? The desire to initiate the sequence of events required to go on a hike or attend a social function? It’s just... absent. It’s like a null value in the system. I don't feel the urge to start anything, and I certainly don't feel the urge to talk to anyone, given the current hostile parameters of my environment. It’s not sadness, exactly, doctor. It’s just a profound, pervasive emptiness where my drive used to be. A complete flattening of the emotional curve, if you will. And yes, that has been a consistent state of affairs for well over a month now, running concurrently with the... the other issues we've discussed.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the negative symptom of markedly reduced motivation/emotional expression has been present for at least one month independent of the persecutory delusion, which would support schizophrenia over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: For at least one full month, have you had this loss of motivation and emotional flatness?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: These days I can sit for hours at my desk or in the garage with the telescope still covered, knowing I used to enjoy hiking, mentoring the younger analysts, and going to astronomy nights, but I just don’t feel much pull to start anything or talk to anyone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about the duration and presence of the loss of motivation and emotional flatness, which corresponds to the negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, doctor, as I... as I believe I just articulated a moment ago, we are well past the thirty-day mark on this particular data point. It has been a full month, absolutely. Probably closer to six weeks, if we were to graph it out accurately. 

As I was saying, I find myself in this state where I can just sit there. For hours at a time. I'll sit at my desk, or I'll go out to the garage, and the telescope—the Schmidt-Cassegrain I mentioned—it just sits there with the dust cover still on it. I can stare at it, and I know, intellectually, that I used to derive a significant amount of satisfaction from it. Going to the local astronomy nights, calibrating the lenses, explaining the orbital mechanics to the public... I know the data says I enjoyed that. Just like I know I used to enjoy hiking up the ridge and mapping out the elevation gains, or... or mentoring the younger analysts at the firm, back before the workplace dynamics shifted so drastically against me. 

But these days? I just don’t feel much pull to start anything. It's like a complete failure in the initiation sequence of my brain. There's no internal spark to begin an activity, and frankly, I don't feel any pull to talk to anyone either. The desire to engage, to initiate a project, to converse... it has just flatlined. It's a persistent, daily reality. So, yes, to confirm your specific timeline, it has absolutely been at least one full month of this... this null state.

inference.note: Ruled out F22 because there has been at least one month of persecutory delusions plus another characteristic schizophrenic symptom (negative symptoms: emotional flatness/avolition) with functional decline; this supports schizophrenia, paranoid type, over delusional disorder.
